stem: You are on `main` and run `git switch -c feature`. What does Git do?

options.text: It copies the working tree into a new `feature/` directory and switches to it
options.why: Git never copies files to create a branch; a branch is just a pointer to a commit.

options.text: It creates a `feature` ref at the current commit and checks it out
options.why: Branch creation writes one small ref; your files stay exactly as they are.

options.text: It creates `feature` from `origin/main` but leaves you on `main`
options.why: That would need an explicit start point, and `switch -c` also switches to the new branch.

options.text: It creates `feature` only after your next commit is made
options.why: The ref exists immediately and points at the current HEAD commit.

explanation: A branch is a lightweight movable pointer (a ref under `.git/refs/heads/`) to a commit. `git switch -c <name>`, like `git checkout -b <name>`, creates that pointer at HEAD and checks it out. No files are copied and the working tree is unchanged; your next commit simply moves the new pointer forward.
reference: Pro Git: Branches in a Nutshell

stem: Creating a new Git branch duplicates every tracked file in the repository, which is why branching is expensive in large repositories.

options.text: True
options.why: Branching in Git does not copy files; this describes older VCS tools such as SVN branch copies.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: a Git branch is a 41-byte ref that points to a commit, so creating one is nearly instant.

explanation: A Git branch is just a reference containing a commit hash. Creating, switching and deleting branches are cheap regardless of repository size; the commits and their trees are shared, content-addressed objects.
reference: Pro Git: Branches in a Nutshell

stem: You are on `main` and run `git branch -d feat`. `feat` has two commits that are not reachable from `main`. What happens?

options.text: The branch is deleted and its two commits are removed from the repository at once
options.why: `-d` refuses here, and even a forced delete leaves the commits in the object store until GC.

options.text: Git merges `feat` into `main` first, then deletes the branch
options.why: Branch deletion never merges anything.

options.text: Git refuses because `feat` is not fully merged, and suggests `git branch -D`
options.why: `-d` is the safe delete: it only deletes branches whose commits are already merged.

options.text: Git deletes the branch but keeps a backup branch named `feat.bak`
options.why: Git creates no backup branch; recovery would need the reflog.

explanation: `git branch -d` deletes a branch only if it is fully merged into its upstream or, if it has none, into HEAD. Otherwise it stops with "error: the branch 'feat' is not fully merged" and hints at `git branch -D`, which forces the deletion. Even after `-D`, the commits remain recoverable through the reflog until garbage collection.

stem: Complete the command that renames the currently checked-out branch to `main`: `git branch ___ main`. Type only the flag.
explanation: `git branch -m <new>` renames the current branch (or `git branch -m <old> <new>` for another branch). `-M` forces the rename even if `<new>` already exists. Renaming moves the ref and its reflog; the remote still has the old name until you push the new one and delete the old.

stem:
History looks like this, and `main` has not moved since `feat` was created:

```
A---B   main
     \
      C---D   feat
```

What happens when you run `git merge feat` on `main`?

options.text: `main` fast-forwards to D, and no merge commit is created
options.why: B is an ancestor of D, so Git just moves the `main` pointer forward.

options.text: Git creates merge commit E with parents B and D
options.why: That only happens with `--no-ff` or when the branches have diverged.

options.text: Git copies C and D onto `main` as new commits C' and D'
options.why: Copying commits is what rebase or cherry-pick does, not a merge.

options.text: Git refuses, because `feat` must be rebased onto `main` first
options.why: No rebase is needed; this is the simplest possible merge.

explanation: When the current branch tip is an ancestor of the branch being merged, there is nothing to combine. Git performs a fast-forward: it moves `main` to D and prints "Fast-forward". History stays linear and no merge commit is made unless you pass `--no-ff`.
reference: Pro Git: Basic Branching and Merging

stem:
A merge of `feat` into `main` stops with this in `x.txt`:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
mainline
=======
feature
>>>>>>> feat
```

Which version is `mainline`?

options.text: The common ancestor's version of the line
options.why: The base only appears with the diff3 or zdiff3 conflict style, between `|||||||` markers.

options.text: The version from `feat`, the branch being merged in
options.why: `feat`'s version is below `=======`, labelled by the `>>>>>>> feat` marker.

options.text: The version from `main`, the branch you are on
options.why: The section after `<<<<<<< HEAD` is always the current branch's side.

options.text: A version Git wrote by combining both edits
options.why: Git does not invent combined text; it shows both sides for you to resolve.

explanation: In the default "merge" conflict style, the hunk between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is your side (the checked-out branch, "ours"). The hunk between `=======` and `>>>>>>> feat` is the branch being merged ("theirs"). You edit the file to the desired content, remove the markers, `git add` it and conclude the merge.

stem: Match each command with what it does.

options.text: List local branches and mark the current one with `*`
options.why: Shown by `git branch`.

options.text: Create a branch and switch to it in one step
options.why: Shown by `git switch -c x`.

options.text: Delete a branch even if it is not merged
options.why: Shown by `git branch -D x`.

options.text: Stop an in-progress merge and restore the pre-merge state
options.why: Shown by `git merge --abort`.

explanation: `git branch` with no arguments lists branches. `git switch -c` (or `git checkout -b`) creates and switches. `-D` is shorthand for `--delete --force`. `git merge --abort` tries to reconstruct the state before the merge started, which only works cleanly if you had no uncommitted changes when you began.

stem: Which two statements about Git branches are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: A branch is a ref that stores the hash of one commit
options.why: That pointer is all a branch is; it moves when you commit.

options.text: HEAD normally points to the branch that is currently checked out
options.why: HEAD is a symbolic ref such as `ref: refs/heads/main`.

options.text: Each branch keeps its own full copy of the project files
options.why: Commits and trees are shared objects; branches copy nothing.

options.text: Deleting a branch immediately erases its commits from disk
options.why: The commits stay until they are unreachable from every ref and reflog and GC runs.

options.text: New branches can only be created from the default branch
options.why: You can start a branch at any commit, tag or other branch.

explanation: Branches are cheap pointers stored as refs, and HEAD usually refers to one of them. Because objects are shared and content-addressed, branching duplicates nothing, and deleting a branch only removes the pointer; unreachable commits are cleaned up later by garbage collection.
reference: Pro Git: Branches in a Nutshell

stem: On `main` you have an uncommitted edit to `a.txt`. Branch `other` differs from `main` only in `b.txt`. What does `git switch other` do?

options.text: It refuses until you commit or stash the uncommitted edit to `a.txt` first
options.why: Git only refuses when the switch would overwrite your local change.

options.text: It switches and silently discards the edit to `a.txt`
options.why: Git never throws away uncommitted work during a normal switch.

options.text: It switches and commits the edit to `a.txt` on `other`
options.why: Switching never creates commits.

options.text: It switches and keeps your edit to `a.txt` in the working tree
options.why: `a.txt` is identical on both branches, so the local change is carried over.

explanation: When a file is the same in the current and target commits, Git can switch without touching it, so your uncommitted modification comes along ("M a.txt / Switched to branch 'other'"). Only files that differ between the two commits and also have local changes block the switch.

stem: On `main` you have an uncommitted edit to `b.txt`. Branch `other` has a committed change to `b.txt`. What does `git switch other` do?

options.text: It aborts, saying your changes to `b.txt` would be overwritten
options.why: Switching would replace `b.txt`, so Git protects your edit and stops.

options.text: It switches and leaves conflict markers in `b.txt`
options.why: That only happens with `git switch -m`; a plain switch refuses.

options.text: It switches and keeps your edit, discarding `other`'s version of `b.txt`
options.why: Git won't silently drop committed content from the target branch either.

options.text: It stashes the edit automatically and switches
options.why: Plain `switch` doesn't stash; you must stash or commit yourself.

explanation: If a file has local modifications and also differs between HEAD and the target branch, switching would overwrite those modifications, so Git aborts with "would be overwritten by checkout". Commit, stash, or use `git switch -m` to attempt a three-way merge of your local changes.

stem: `feat` could be fast-forwarded into `main`, but you run `git merge --no-ff feat -m "merge feat"`. What does `git log --graph --format=%s` show afterwards?

options.text: `c2` above `c1` in a straight line, because a fast-forward happened anyway
options.why: `--no-ff` explicitly forbids the fast-forward.

options.text: Only `merge feat`, because the branch commits are squashed
options.why: Squashing is `--squash`; `--no-ff` keeps every commit.

options.text: A `merge feat` commit with two parents: `c1` and the branch commit `c2`
options.why: A merge commit is created so the branch's existence stays visible.

options.text: An error, because `--no-ff` needs the branches to have diverged
options.why: `--no-ff` works whether or not a fast-forward is possible.

explanation:
Verified output:

```
*   merge feat
|\
| * c2
|/
* c1
```

`--no-ff` always records a merge commit, keeping the feature's commits grouped as a side branch. Teams use it so `git log --first-parent main` shows one entry per merged feature.

stem: `main` and `feat` have each gained a commit since they split. What does `git merge --ff-only feat` do?

options.text: It creates a normal merge commit because fast-forward is impossible
options.why: `--ff-only` never falls back to a merge commit.

options.text: It rebases `main` onto `feat` first and then fast-forwards
options.why: Git doesn't rebase for you during a merge.

options.text: It fast-forwards `main` to `feat`, dropping `main`'s extra commit
options.why: A fast-forward can never discard commits; that's why it's impossible here.

options.text: It fails: "Not possible to fast-forward, aborting"
options.why: With diverged histories there is no fast-forward to perform.

explanation: `--ff-only` succeeds only when HEAD is an ancestor of the merged commit. With diverged history Git prints hints (merge with `--no-ff` or rebase) and "fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting.", leaving the branch untouched. It's a common safety setting for updating a local branch from its upstream.

stem: Running `git merge --squash feat` creates a merge commit whose second parent is the tip of `feat`.

options.text: True
options.why: A squash merge records no merge relationship at all.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: it only updates the index and working tree; you then make an ordinary single-parent commit.

explanation: `--squash` produces the combined changes in the index without committing and without setting MERGE_HEAD (verified: `status` shows `M  f.txt`, no MERGE_HEAD). The commit you make has one parent, so Git has no record that `feat` was merged.

stem: During a conflicted merge, `git status --short` shows `UU x.txt`. What does `UU` mean?

options.text: `x.txt` is untracked on both branches
options.why: Untracked files show as `??`.

options.text: `x.txt` is unmerged and was modified on both sides
options.why: U in both columns means both modified, conflict not yet resolved.

options.text: `x.txt` was updated in the index and the working tree, with no conflict
options.why: A staged and modified file shows as `MM`.

options.text: `x.txt` was deleted on both branches
options.why: Both deleted shows as `DD`.

explanation: In short status, unmerged paths use codes such as `UU` (both modified), `AA` (both added), `UD` (modified by us, deleted by them) and `DU`. The path stays unmerged until you `git add` (or `git rm`) it after resolving.

stem: Which two commands delete the branch `feature` on the remote `origin`? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git push origin --delete feature`
options.why: The explicit, readable form of deleting a remote branch.

options.text: `git push origin :feature`
options.why: Pushing an empty source to a ref deletes it; this is the older refspec form.

options.text: `git branch -D feature`
options.why: This only deletes your local branch.

options.text: `git branch -d origin/feature`
options.why: That names a remote-tracking ref, not a local branch, and never touches the server.

options.text: `git fetch --prune feature`
options.why: Pruning only removes stale remote-tracking refs locally.

explanation: Remote branches are deleted by pushing a deletion: `git push origin --delete feature` or `git push origin :feature`. Local deletion with `git branch -d/-D` and pruning remote-tracking refs with `git fetch --prune` don't change the server.

stem: Put the steps for finishing a merge that stopped on a conflict in `x.txt` in order.

options.text: Run `git merge feat` and see the CONFLICT message
options.why: Starts the merge.

options.text: Edit `x.txt` to the final content and remove the markers
options.why: Resolves the content.

options.text: Run `git add x.txt` to mark it resolved
options.why: Moves it from unmerged to staged.

options.text: Run `git merge --continue` (or `git commit`)
options.why: Creates the merge commit.

explanation: Git can't record the merge while any path is unmerged: `git merge --continue` fails with "Committing is not possible because you have unmerged files" until each conflicted file is resolved and added. After `git add`, `--continue` (or a plain `git commit`) creates the merge commit with both parents.

stem: In a three-way merge of `feat` into `main`, what is the merge base?

options.text: The root commit, since every branch ultimately starts from it
options.why: The root commit is rarely the best common ancestor.

options.text: The current tip of `main`, because that is where the merge result goes
options.why: That is "ours", one of the two sides, not the base.

options.text: Whichever commit `origin/main` pointed to at your last fetch
options.why: Remote-tracking refs play no role in choosing the base.

options.text: The best common ancestor of both tips (`git merge-base main feat`)
options.why: Both sides' changes are computed relative to this commit.

explanation: A three-way merge compares each tip against their best common ancestor. A change made on only one side is taken automatically; changes to the same region on both sides become conflicts. `git merge-base A B` prints that ancestor.

stem: What does `git branch --merged` list?

options.text: Branches whose tips are reachable from HEAD
options.why: Their commits are already in the current branch, so `-d` would succeed.

options.text: Branches that were merged using a merge commit
options.why: Fast-forwarded branches count too; only reachability matters.

options.text: Branches that have been pushed to a remote
options.why: Push status isn't part of this check.

options.text: Branches that were squash-merged on GitHub
options.why: Squash merges leave the branch tip unreachable, so they show under `--no-merged`.

explanation: `--merged` filters to branches whose tip commit is an ancestor of HEAD (or of a commit you name). It's a handy way to find branches safe to delete with `git branch -d`. Squash and rebase merges create new commits, so the original branch still appears as unmerged.

stem: Since Git 2.34, what is the name of the default strategy `git merge` uses when merging a single branch? Type the strategy name.
explanation: Git 2.33 introduced the "ort" strategy ("Ostensibly Recursive's Twin") and 2.34 made it the default, replacing "recursive". Merge output shows "Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.". It handles renames and criss-cross merges like recursive but is much faster.

stem: From a common base, `feat` changed line 2 of `a.txt`, changed `b.txt`, and added `c.txt`. `main` changed the same line 2 of `a.txt` differently. On `main` you run `git merge -X ours feat`. What is the result?

options.text: The tree is identical to `main`; `b.txt` and `c.txt` changes are dropped
options.why: That describes the `-s ours` strategy, not the `-X ours` option.

options.text: `a.txt` keeps `main`'s line 2; `b.txt` and `c.txt` take `feat`'s changes
options.why: `-X ours` only decides conflicting hunks; everything else merges normally.

options.text: The merge stops with a conflict in `a.txt`, exactly as a plain merge would
options.why: `-X ours` auto-resolves conflicting hunks instead of stopping.

options.text: All three files take `feat`'s version, because `feat` is newer
options.why: Commit dates don't matter, and `-X ours` favours the current branch.

explanation: Verified: after `git merge -X ours feat`, `a.txt` contains `MAIN` on line 2, `b.txt` is `b-feat` and `c.txt` exists. The `-X ours` strategy option tells ort to resolve conflicting hunks in favour of the current branch; non-conflicting changes from the other side are still merged.

stem: Same history as before: `feat` changed `a.txt` and `b.txt` and added `c.txt`, while `main` changed `a.txt`. You run `git merge -s ours feat` on `main`. Which describes the result?

options.text: Conflicting lines in `a.txt` keep `main`'s side; other changes from `feat` merge in
options.why: That is the `-X ours` option; `-s ours` ignores the other branch entirely.

options.text: Git fast-forwards `main` to `feat`, then reverts the conflicting change
options.why: The ours strategy never fast-forwards or reverts.

options.text: Git refuses, because `-s ours` works only when there are conflicts
options.why: The strategy works regardless of conflicts.

options.text: A merge commit whose tree equals `main`'s, with `feat` recorded as a second parent
options.why: All of `feat`'s changes are discarded, but history says it was merged.

explanation: Verified: after `-s ours`, `a.txt` is unchanged, `b.txt` is still `b0`, `c.txt` doesn't exist, and the commit has two parents. `git branch --merged` then lists `feat`. The ours strategy is used to supersede an old branch while marking it merged, e.g. to stop it being merged later.

stem: `a.txt` has 7 lines. `feat` changed lines 1 and 7; `main` changed only line 1. You run `git merge -X ours feat` on `main`. What are lines 1 and 7 afterwards?

options.text: Line 1 from `main` and line 7 unchanged from the base
options.why: Line 7 has no conflict, so `feat`'s change to it is merged.

options.text: Line 1 from `feat` and line 7 from `feat`
options.why: `-X ours` makes the conflicting line 1 keep `main`'s side.

options.text: Line 1 from `main` and line 7 from `feat`
options.why: Only the overlapping hunk is resolved to ours; the other hunk merges cleanly.

options.text: Conflict markers around line 1, and line 7 from `feat`
options.why: The strategy option resolves conflicts automatically, so no markers appear.

explanation: Verified result: `L1-main` on line 1 and `L7-feat` on line 7. `-X ours`/`-X theirs` work hunk by hunk within a file, not file by file. If you wanted the whole file from one side, you would use `git checkout --ours <file>` during a normal conflicted merge.

stem: You squash-merged `feat` into `main` last week. Since then `feat` gained one more commit and `main` edited the same line. Now `git merge feat` conflicts on changes that were already squashed in. Why?

options.text: Squash merges corrupt the index, so Git loses track of which lines `feat` changed
options.why: Nothing is corrupted; the history is simply missing a link.

options.text: The ort strategy cannot merge a branch twice
options.why: Branches can be merged repeatedly when ancestry is recorded.

options.text: The squash commit was signed, so Git treats it as immutable
options.why: Signatures have no effect on merge bases.

options.text: The squash commit has one parent, so the merge base is still the old fork point
options.why: `feat`'s already-squashed changes are compared again against `main`'s edits.

explanation: Because `--squash` records no merge parent, `git merge-base main feat` still returns the commit where `feat` started. The next merge replays all of `feat`'s changes relative to that old base, colliding with the squashed copy plus anything `main` changed since. Delete squash-merged branches, or rebase the remaining work onto `main` before continuing.

stem: After `git merge --squash feat` and `git commit` on `main`, you run `git branch -d feat`. What happens?

options.text: It refuses: `feat`'s tip isn't reachable from `main`, so it isn't merged
options.why: The squash commit is new; `feat`'s commits are not ancestors of `main`.

options.text: It deletes `feat`, because Git sees that its changes are already in `main`
options.why: `-d` checks reachability of commits, not whether the content matches.

options.text: It deletes `feat` and its commits are also squashed away
options.why: Deleting a branch never rewrites commits.

options.text: It asks whether you want to delete the squash commit too
options.why: Branch deletion is non-interactive and doesn't touch other commits.

explanation: Verified: `error: the branch 'feat' is not fully merged`. Content equality doesn't count; `-d` only checks whether the branch tip is reachable. After a squash or rebase merge you use `git branch -D` once you're sure the work landed.

stem: You are on `main` merging `feat`, and `x.txt` conflicts: `main` has `mainline`, `feat` has `feature`. You run `git checkout --theirs x.txt`. What does `x.txt` contain?

options.text: `mainline`
options.why: That is "ours" during a merge: the branch you are on.

options.text: `feature`
options.why: In a merge, "theirs" is the branch being merged in.

options.text: The common ancestor's content
options.why: Use `--conflict=diff3` or `git show :1:x.txt` to see the base.

options.text: The conflicted file with markers left in place
options.why: `--theirs` replaces the file with one side's version.

explanation: Verified: the file becomes `feature`. During a merge, stage 2 ("ours") is HEAD and stage 3 ("theirs") is MERGE_HEAD. The file is still marked unmerged until you `git add` it.

stem: On `feat` you run `git rebase main` and `x.txt` conflicts: `main` has `mainline`, `feat`'s commit has `feature`. You run `git checkout --ours x.txt`. What does `x.txt` contain?

options.text: `feature`, because you started the rebase from `feat`, so it is "ours"
options.why: During a rebase, "ours" is the base being built on, not your branch.

options.text: The common ancestor's content
options.why: `--ours` picks one side, never the base.

options.text: Nothing: `--ours` is rejected during a rebase
options.why: It works during a rebase; only its meaning is flipped.

options.text: `mainline`: during a rebase, "ours" is the branch you replay onto
options.why: Rebase replays your commits onto `main`, so HEAD is the rebased-so-far history.

explanation: Verified: `mainline`. A rebase checks out `main` and cherry-picks your commits onto it, so HEAD ("ours") is the upstream side and the commit being replayed is "theirs". This reversal compared with merges is one of Git's most common surprises.

stem: A merge stopped with an unresolved conflict in `x.txt`. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git merge --abort` restores the branch and files to their state before the merge
options.why: Abort undoes the merge attempt when you had no uncommitted changes beforehand.

options.text: `git merge --continue` fails while `x.txt` is still unmerged
options.why: Git refuses: "Committing is not possible because you have unmerged files."

options.text: `git merge --continue` resolves the remaining conflict using HEAD's version
options.why: Git never resolves conflicts for you on continue.

options.text: `git merge --abort` deletes the branch that was being merged
options.why: The merged branch is untouched.

options.text: After `--abort`, MERGE_HEAD still exists so you can resume later
options.why: Abort removes the merge state entirely.

explanation: Verified: `--continue` with an unmerged path exits with "fatal: Exiting because of an unresolved conflict", and `--abort` returns `x.txt` to `mainline` with a clean status. To resume work later you would resolve, `git add`, then `--continue`.

stem: You set `merge.conflictStyle = zdiff3` (or diff3). What extra information appears in conflicted hunks?

options.text: The author and date of each conflicting commit
options.why: Conflict markers never include authorship.

options.text: A suggested automatic resolution between the markers
options.why: Git only shows the versions; it doesn't suggest a resolution.

options.text: A `|||||||` section with the common ancestor's version
options.why: Seeing the base shows what each side actually changed.

options.text: The full file from both branches instead of just the hunk
options.why: Markers still surround only the conflicting region.

explanation:
Verified output:

```
<<<<<<< ours
mainline
||||||| base
base
=======
feature
>>>>>>> theirs
```

With the base visible you can tell whether a side changed or deleted a line, which makes resolutions far less error-prone. `zdiff3` additionally moves lines common to both sides outside the conflict region.

stem: Match each merge command with its effect on `main` when merging `feat`.

options.text: Result tree equals `main`; `feat` is recorded as a parent
options.why: This is the ours strategy.

options.text: Conflicting hunks take `main`'s side; other changes merge normally
options.why: This is the ours strategy option.

options.text: Conflicting hunks take `feat`'s side; other changes merge normally
options.why: This is the theirs strategy option.

options.text: Combined changes are staged; no merge commit and no MERGE_HEAD
options.why: This is a squash merge.

explanation: `-s` selects a whole merge strategy; `-X` passes an option to the default strategy. That is why `-s ours` discards the other side completely while `-X ours` only breaks ties. There is no `-s theirs`. A squash merge stages the combined result but records no merge relationship.

stem: `feat` changed `a.txt`. `main` changed `b.txt`, and you also have an uncommitted edit to `b.txt`. What does `git merge feat` do?

options.text: It aborts because the working tree is dirty
options.why: Git only aborts when the merge needs to modify a file you've changed.

options.text: It merges and overwrites your edit to `b.txt` with `main`'s committed version
options.why: Git never discards your uncommitted edits during a merge.

options.text: It merges, and your `b.txt` edit stays uncommitted in the working tree
options.why: The merge doesn't touch `b.txt`, so the local edit is preserved.

options.text: It includes your `b.txt` edit in the merge commit
options.why: Merge commits only contain the merge result, not unstaged edits.

explanation: Verified: "Merge made by the 'ort' strategy" and `b.txt` still contains the local edit. Had the merge needed to change `a.txt` while it was dirty, Git would have aborted with "Your local changes ... would be overwritten by merge". Still, merging with a clean tree is safer because `--abort` can't always restore uncommitted changes.

stem: Git has a `-s theirs` merge strategy that is the mirror image of `-s ours`, producing a tree identical to the other branch.

options.text: True
options.why: No such strategy exists; Git reports "Could not find merge strategy 'theirs'."

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: only `-s ours` exists. `-X theirs` is a strategy option that affects only conflicting hunks.

explanation: Verified: `git merge -s theirs x` fails and lists the available strategies (octopus, ours, recursive, resolve, subtree). To make a branch match another's tree while recording a merge, merge with `-s ours` from the other side, or use `git merge --no-commit` and then `git read-tree`/`git checkout <other> -- .` before committing.

stem: A merge stops and `git status --short` shows `UD a.txt`. `main` modified `a.txt`; `feat` deleted it. How do you resolve it?

options.text: Edit out the conflict markers in `a.txt`, then `git add` it
options.why: A modify/delete conflict has no markers; the whole file is in question.

options.text: Run `git merge --continue`; Git keeps the modified version automatically
options.why: Continue fails while the path is unmerged.

options.text: Run `git checkout --theirs a.txt` to restore the deleted file
options.why: "Theirs" deleted it, so there is no theirs version to check out.

options.text: Keep it with `git add a.txt` or delete it with `git rm a.txt`
options.why: Your choice of add or rm records the resolution.

explanation: Verified: "CONFLICT (modify/delete): a.txt deleted in f and modified in HEAD. Version HEAD of a.txt left in tree." `UD` means updated by us, deleted by them. You decide the file's fate with `git add` (keep) or `git rm` (delete), then `git merge --continue`.

stem: You have an uncommitted edit to `b.txt` and run `git switch -m other`, where `other` also changed `b.txt`. What happens?

options.text: It refuses exactly like a plain `git switch`
options.why: `-m` exists precisely to avoid that refusal.

options.text: It switches and throws away the local edit to `b.txt`
options.why: `-m` merges your edit; it doesn't discard it.

options.text: It commits the local edit on `main`, then switches
options.why: `switch` never creates commits.

options.text: It switches and leaves `b.txt` with conflict markers
options.why: Git tries a three-way merge of your local changes into the new branch.

explanation: Verified: `b.txt` contains `<<<<<<< other` / `b-other` / `=======` / `b-dirty` / `>>>>>>> local`, and status shows `UU b.txt`. With `-m`, Git switches and merges your uncommitted changes into the target; conflicts are left for you to resolve, and the pre-switch version of your edit isn't kept anywhere else.

stem: With `rerere.enabled = true`, you resolved a conflict in `x.txt` and committed. You then `git reset --hard HEAD~1` and run the same merge again. Git prints "Resolved 'x.txt' using previous resolution." What is the state of `x.txt`?

options.text: It holds conflict markers, because rerere only records resolutions
options.why: Rerere replays the resolution into the working tree.

options.text: It holds the resolution, and the merge was committed automatically
options.why: Rerere never commits.

options.text: It holds the earlier resolution but stays unmerged until you `git add` it
options.why: Without `rerere.autoUpdate`, the index isn't updated for you.

options.text: It holds `main`'s version, because the reset removed the recorded resolution
options.why: Recorded resolutions live in `.git/rr-cache`, which reset doesn't touch.

explanation: Verified: the file contains `resolved` but `git status --short` shows `UU x.txt`. Rerere ("reuse recorded resolution") rewrites the working tree from its cache but leaves staging to you, so you can review it. Set `rerere.autoUpdate = true` to have Git stage reused resolutions automatically.

stem: Two branches merged into each other at different points (a criss-cross), and `git merge-base --all main B` prints two commits. How does Git's default strategy merge `B` into `main`?

options.text: It picks the newer of the two merge bases and ignores the other
options.why: That is what the older "resolve" strategy does when it picks one base.

options.text: It merges the two bases into a virtual ancestor and uses that
options.why: ort, like recursive, builds a synthetic base when there are several.

options.text: It refuses and asks you to choose a base with `--base`
options.why: There's no such option; Git handles multiple bases itself.

options.text: It falls back to a two-way merge with no base, conflicting on every change
options.why: A two-way merge would make every difference a conflict; Git avoids that.

explanation: Verified: `merge-base --all` returned two commits after the criss-cross. ort and recursive merge the common ancestors (recursively, if needed) into a virtual merge base, which usually gives fewer spurious conflicts than picking one arbitrarily. Conflicts inside that virtual base can surface as nested markers.

stem: You run `git merge b1 b2 b3`, and `b1` and `b2` both change the same line of `a.txt`. What happens?

options.text: Git creates an octopus merge and leaves markers for you to resolve
options.why: Octopus doesn't support manual conflict resolution.

options.text: Git merges `b1` and `b3`, then skips `b2`
options.why: Octopus never silently skips a branch.

options.text: Git resolves the line in favour of the last branch listed
options.why: There's no last-one-wins rule.

options.text: The octopus strategy refuses, and the merge fails
options.why: Octopus is only for merges that resolve cleanly.

explanation: Verified: "Automated merge did not work. Should not be doing an octopus. ... Merge with strategy octopus failed." The octopus strategy, the default for more than two heads, refuses complex merges needing manual resolution. Merge the conflicting branches one at a time instead.

stem: `main` is an ancestor of `b3` (it hasn't diverged from it), and `b4` is a separate branch off `main`. You run `git merge b3 b4 -m oct` on `main`. How many parents does the resulting commit have?

options.text: Two: Git first fast-forwards to `b3`, then merges `b4`
options.why: Fast-forwarding past `main` removes it as a separate parent.

options.text: Three: `main`, `b3` and `b4`, as in any octopus merge
options.why: That holds only when `main` has diverged from the branches.

options.text: One: the octopus merge squashes everything
options.why: Octopus records each merged head as a parent.

options.text: None: Git refuses an octopus merge when a fast-forward is possible
options.why: It doesn't refuse; it fast-forwards and continues.

explanation: Verified: Git printed "Fast-forwarding to: b3", then "Trying simple merge with b4", and the merge commit has 2 parents. When the current branch is behind one of the named heads, octopus fast-forwards to it first. With `--no-ff` you would get `main` as an explicit parent too.

stem: `main`, `p` and `q` have all diverged from a common commit, and none of the changes overlap. On `main` you run `git merge p q -m oct`. How many parents does the new commit have? Type a number.
explanation: Verified: "Merge made by the 'octopus' strategy." with 3 parents (`main`, `p`, `q`). Octopus merges record one parent per merged head plus the current branch, which is why `git log --first-parent` and `^2`/`^3` notation matter in repositories that use them.

stem: Branch A renames `getUser()` to `fetchUser()` everywhere. Branch B, created earlier, adds a new call to `getUser()` in a different file. Both merge into `main` without any conflict, but the build fails. Why, and what prevents it?

options.text: ort mis-merged the code; switching to `-s resolve` would have flagged the conflict
options.why: No strategy understands code semantics; they all merge text.

options.text: Git should have reported a rename conflict, and enabling rerere would catch it next time
options.why: This isn't a file rename, and rerere only replays recorded resolutions.

options.text: Merges are textual; catch semantic conflicts by testing the merged result in CI
options.why: Only compiling and testing the combined code reveals it.

options.text: B should have used `--no-ff` so Git would notice the dangling call
options.why: Merge mode doesn't change how content is combined.

explanation: Git compares lines, not meaning. Changes in different places merge cleanly even when they are logically incompatible, a "semantic conflict". Protections include running CI on the merged result (merge queues, required up-to-date branches) and keeping branches short-lived.

stem: During a conflicted merge of `feat`, how does `git checkout --theirs .` differ from having run `git merge -X theirs feat`?

options.text: They are equivalent: both take `feat`'s version of each file that had a conflict
options.why: `-X theirs` works per hunk, while checkout replaces whole files.

options.text: Checkout takes `feat`'s whole file; `-X theirs` only settles conflicting hunks
options.why: With `-X theirs`, `main`'s non-conflicting changes in the same file survive.

options.text: `-X theirs` takes whole files, while checkout only fixes conflicting hunks
options.why: This is the reverse of the real behaviour.

options.text: Checkout also stages the files, whereas `-X theirs` leaves them unmerged
options.why: Checkout leaves paths unmerged until `git add`; `-X theirs` resolves them during the merge.

explanation: `git checkout --theirs <path>` copies stage 3 (the merged-in version) of the file, discarding `main`'s changes even in parts of the file that didn't conflict. `-X theirs` keeps non-conflicting hunks from both sides and favours `feat` only where hunks overlap. Pick based on whether you want whole-file or hunk-level preference.

stem: On `main` you run `git merge -s ours old-feature` to retire an obsolete branch. Which two statements are true afterwards? (Choose two.)

options.text: None of `old-feature`'s file changes are in `main`
options.why: The ours strategy keeps the current tree exactly.

options.text: `git branch --merged` lists `old-feature`
options.why: Its tip is now a parent of `main`, so it is reachable.

options.text: The merge commit has a single parent
options.why: It records both `main` and `old-feature` as parents.

options.text: Merging `old-feature` again later reapplies its changes
options.why: It's already an ancestor, so Git reports "Already up to date".

options.text: The command fails unless there are conflicts
options.why: `-s ours` works whether or not the branches conflict.

explanation: Verified: after `-s ours` the tree matches `main`, the commit has two parents, and `git branch --merged` includes the merged branch. Because its commits are now ancestors, any later merge of that branch is a no-op, which is exactly why teams use `-s ours` to supersede history deliberately.

stem: Put the steps of a three-way merge in the order Git performs them.

options.text: Find the merge base of the two tips
options.why: Comes first.

options.text: Diff the base against each tip
options.why: Needs the base.

options.text: Apply changes that only one side made
options.why: Uses both diffs.

options.text: Mark regions both sides changed differently as conflicts
options.why: Comes last.

explanation: Git first computes the merge base (synthesising a virtual one if there are several), then compares base→ours and base→theirs. Changes on only one side are taken; identical changes on both sides are taken once; overlapping different changes become conflicts left for you with markers.

stem: `img.bin` is a binary file changed differently on `main` and `feat`. What is in the working-tree `img.bin` after `git merge feat` reports a conflict?

options.text: A text file with conflict markers around both binary blobs
options.why: Git doesn't write markers into files it treats as binary.

options.text: An empty file, because Git can't choose a version
options.why: Git leaves a valid file in place.

options.text: `feat`'s version, because the merged-in side wins for binaries
options.why: Git keeps the current branch's file, not theirs.

options.text: The unchanged `main` version, with the path left unmerged
options.why: Git warns "Cannot merge binary files" and keeps HEAD's copy.

explanation: Verified: "warning: Cannot merge binary files: img.bin (HEAD vs. feat)" and the file bytes are still `main`'s. Resolve by picking a side with `git checkout --ours/--theirs img.bin` (or providing a new file), then `git add` it. A custom merge driver in `.gitattributes` can automate this for specific formats.

stem: You renamed `master` to `main` locally, ran `git push -u origin main`, and then ran `git push origin --delete master`. GitHub rejects the delete with "refusing to delete the current branch". What must you do first?

options.text: Run `git branch -D master` locally, which also unlocks the remote branch
options.why: Local refs don't affect what the server allows.

options.text: Change the repository's default branch to `main` on GitHub
options.why: The server won't delete the branch its HEAD points to.

options.text: Force the delete with `git push --force origin --delete master`
options.why: Forcing doesn't override the server's protection of its default branch.

options.text: Re-run the rename with `git branch -M`, which also updates the remote
options.why: Renaming is local only; the server keeps the old name.

explanation: A bare remote's HEAD points at its default branch, and the server refuses to delete it. Switch the default branch in the hosting settings (or GitHub's rename feature, which also updates redirects and open PRs), then delete the old branch. Teammates update with `git fetch`, `git branch -u origin/main main` and `git remote set-head origin -a`.

stem: A repository sets `git config merge.ff false`. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git merge feat` creates a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible
options.why: The setting makes every merge behave like `--no-ff`.

options.text: `git merge --ff-only feat` still fast-forwards when that is possible
options.why: A command-line flag overrides the config setting.

options.text: Squash merges are no longer allowed
options.why: `merge.ff` doesn't affect `--squash`.

options.text: `git branch -d` now refuses every deletion
options.why: Branch deletion ignores merge settings.

options.text: Nothing can override it for a single merge
options.why: Command-line options like `--ff-only` or `--ff` take precedence.

explanation: Verified: with `merge.ff = false`, a fast-forwardable `git merge f` produced a commit with 2 parents, while `git merge --ff-only f` still fast-forwarded. Config sets the default; command-line flags override it. `merge.ff = only` is the stricter alternative that refuses anything but fast-forwards.
